hang.protocol: Passive bar hang, overhand, shoulder width, legs off the ground, straight arms, until the person dropped. Mean of 3 trials, 3 min rest. Before 6 weeks of training.
hang.result: Mean 64.0 s (SD 35.3); 69.4 s (SD 33.7) after 6 weeks of training
hang.source: Chomiuk et al., J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 2025, Table 2
hang.line: In the GRIP-6 study, 11 healthy recreational-athlete men with a mean age of 20.2 held a passive bar hang for a mean of 64.0 seconds (SD 35.3) before training.

hang.protocol: Same as men. Before 6 weeks of training.
hang.result: Mean 48.4 s (SD 29.1); 54.3 s (SD 28.7) after 6 weeks of training
hang.source: Chomiuk et al., J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 2025, Table 2
hang.line: In the GRIP-6 study, 14 healthy recreational-athlete women with a mean age of 20.6 held a passive bar hang for a mean of 48.4 seconds (SD 29.1) before training.

hang.protocol: Same as above. Before and after 6 weeks of combined gym and climbing training.
hang.result: Mean 55.3 s before and 60.9 s after (+5.6 s, 95% CI 4.0 to 7.3)
hang.source: Chomiuk et al., J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 2025, Table 2
hang.line: The same 25 GRIP-6 participants improved their mean bar hang from 55.3 seconds to 60.9 seconds after 6 weeks of gym and climbing training (change 5.6 s, 95% CI 4.0 to 7.3).

hang.protocol: Straight-arm hang from a standard Olympic bar attached to the top of a power rack. Moderately trained, free of upper-body injury. Each person also hung from a triangular Tri-Bar.
hang.result: Mean 95.4 s on the standard bar; 107.6 s on the Tri-Bar (p = 0.015)
hang.source: Drury, Faggiono and Stuempfle, J Strength Cond Res 2004;18(4):782-786
hang.line: In a 2004 study of 32 moderately trained men, the mean straight-arm hang from a standard Olympic bar was 95.4 seconds, against 107.6 seconds on a triangular Tri-Bar.

hang.dataset: Yu 2023, climbers, porch-edge hang, before a 24-hour event
hang.n: 35 with paired hang data (36 climbers analyzed)
hang.protocol: Static hang to failure from the edge of an elevated wooden porch, feet off the ground. Hand spacing and body position self-selected; most hung on bent fingers. An edge hang, not a bar hang; arm position not stated. Measured at registration, before a 24-hour climbing competition.
hang.result: Mean 76.8 s (SD 32.6) before; 38.1 s (SD 24.9) within an hour after the event
hang.source: Yu et al., Front Sports Act Living 2023
hang.line: In 36 recreational to elite climbers (35 with paired hang data), the mean static hang to failure from a porch edge before a 24-hour climbing event was 76.8 seconds (SD 32.6), falling to 38.1 seconds afterward.

flex.protocol: UNIFITTEST 6-60 bent-arm hang (protocol not described in the paper). Male students without regular organized sport, years 1 to 3 of bachelor study. Bent-arm, not a dead hang.
flex.source: Cepková et al., Front Physiol 2025;16:1634125, Table 2
flex.line: In 88 male university students (mean age 20.1) at the Slovak University of Technology in Bratislava, the mean bent-arm hang was 44.85 seconds (SD 30.64), with a range of 0 to 111 seconds.

flex.protocol: Flexed-arm hang, scored in seconds up to a maximum of 90 s. Score must be at or above the value to reach the Healthy Fitness Zone.
flex.spread: 2 s at age 5; 15 s from age 14
flex.result: At least 2 s at age 5, rising to at least 15 s from age 14
flex.source: California Department of Education, FITNESSGRAM Healthy Fitness Zones, September 2011
flex.line: In the 2011-12 California Physical Fitness Test table (2010 Cooper Institute zones), the flexed-arm hang minimum for the Healthy Fitness Zone was 2 seconds for a 5-year-old boy and 15 seconds from age 14.

flex.spread: 2 s at age 5; 8 s from age 13
flex.result: At least 2 s at age 5, rising to at least 8 s from age 13
flex.source: California Department of Education, FITNESSGRAM Healthy Fitness Zones, September 2011
flex.line: In the 2011-12 California Physical Fitness Test table (2010 Cooper Institute zones), the flexed-arm hang minimum for the Healthy Fitness Zone was 2 seconds for a 5-year-old girl and 8 seconds from age 13.

grip.measure: All-cause mortality, per 5 kg lower grip
grip.sample: 139,691 adults aged 35 to 70 analyzed (142,861 enrolled), 17 countries; 3,379 deaths (2%); median follow-up 4.0 years; Jamar dynamometer
grip.line: In the PURE study, each 5 kg lower grip strength was associated with a 16% higher hazard of all-cause death (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.20) among 139,691 adults in 17 countries.

grip.measure: All-cause mortality, per 5 kg lower grip: women / men
grip.sample: 502,293 participants aged 40 to 69 (54% women); 13,322 deaths (2.7%); mean follow-up 7.1 years
grip.line: In UK Biobank, each 5 kg lower grip strength was associated with a hazard ratio for all-cause death of 1.20 in women and 1.16 in men (502,293 participants aged 40 to 69).

grip.value: 51 kg men (ages 29 to 39); 31 kg women (ages 26 to 42)
grip.sample: 60,803 observations from 49,964 participants (26,687 female), 12 general-population studies in Great Britain, ages 4 to 90; maximum of up to six trials per person, both hands (two studies supplied dominant hand only)
grip.line: Pooled British data from 49,964 participants put peak median grip strength at 51 kg for men aged 29 to 39 and 31 kg for women aged 26 to 42.

grip.sample: Same pooled sample; weak grip defined as 2.5 SD or more below the sex-specific peak mean
grip.line: By age 80, 23% of men and 27% of women in the pooled British data had weak grip, defined as 2.5 SD or more below the sex-specific peak mean.

grip.value: Below 27 kg men; below 16 kg women
grip.sample: Consensus cut-off referenced to Dodds 2014 (T-score of -2.5 or lower)
grip.source: Cruz-Jentoft et al. (EWGSOP2), Age Ageing 2019;48:16-31, Table 3
grip.line: The EWGSOP2 consensus lists low grip strength as below 27 kg for men and below 16 kg for women, referenced to the 2014 British norms.

rec.title: Dead hang position
rec.line: Tazio Gavioli of Italy held the dead hang position for 13 minutes 52 seconds on April 14, 2018, the record Guinness reports Harald Riise later beat.

rec.title: Dead hang position
rec.source: Guinness record page 118967, Wayback copy of May 28, 2022
rec.line: Harald Riise of Norway held the dead hang position for 16 minutes 3 seconds on November 7, 2020.

rec.title: Dead hang position (male)
rec.line: Kenta Adachi of Japan holds the Guinness record for the longest dead hang position at 80 minutes 41 seconds (4,841 seconds), set on November 18, 2022.

rec.title: Oldest person, dead hang position (female)
rec.source: Guinness record page 771587, Wayback copy of May 6, 2025
rec.line: Annie Judis was 80 years 353 days old when she hung for 2 minutes on November 11, 2024 to set the Guinness oldest-woman dead hang record.

rec.title: Hanging from a bar (male)
rec.line: Kenta Adachi holds a separate Guinness title for hanging from a bar at 4 hours 30 minutes 18 seconds (16,218 seconds), set on December 26, 2025.

rec.title: Oldest person, dead hang position (female)
rec.line: Ann Crile Esselstyn was 90 years 231 days old when she held a dead hang for 2 minutes 52 seconds on March 6, 2026, beating the 2024 title.

rec.title: Hanging from a bar (female)
rec.line: Stefanie Millinger of Austria holds the Guinness title for the longest duration hanging from a bar (female) at 53 minutes 51 seconds (3,231 seconds), set on July 11, 2026.

rec.title: Oldest person, dead hang position (female)
rec.line: Ann Crile Esselstyn was 91 years 51 days old when she held a dead hang for 3 minutes 43 seconds on September 7, 2026, the current Guinness oldest-woman record.
